lesson.menu_title: The Post-mortem -- What We Would Have Done
lesson.menu_desc: A manual control on your new map did not run for three days, and nobody lost money. Today you learn the tense English keeps for the thing that did not happen -- and how to say what would have happened without putting a name in the sentence -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- The Post-mortem: What We Would Have Done
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Sergio Takashi Tanaka | Lesson 18 -- The Post-mortem: What We Would Have Done

reading.rtitle: Post-mortem Review -- Exposure Limit Breach, 13-15 July (Ref. PM-22)
paras: This note is the written record of the post-mortem we held on Friday. It is blameless by design. We are not looking for the person who failed; we are looking for the step that failed, and we are writing it down so that the same three days cannot happen twice.

The timeline is short. On Monday the thirteenth, the daily exposure check was not run. The owner of the control was on a plane, the deputy had not been told, and nothing on any screen said that the check was missing. On Tuesday the number passed the limit by four million. It was overlooked for two full days, until a trader on the credit desk noticed it on Wednesday afternoon, by accident, while he was looking for something else. If the alert had covered the manual controls as well, we would have seen it on Monday afternoon. If the deputy had been told on Friday the tenth, the check would have run on time and there would have been no breach at all.

We should have marked this control as manual on the map we sent in June, and we should have named the deputy on the same line. We could have used the automated alert as a workaround while the manual check was down, and nobody thought of it, because nobody knew the check was down. It is easy to say in hindsight; it was not obvious on the day. That is the point of writing it here.

Two things stop this being a lucky escape and make it useful. First, we traced the problem back to a single lapse: an out-of-office message that nobody read. Second, we are calling this what it is -- a near miss. The market moved back on Thursday and we lost nothing, which is exactly why it is dangerous: a quarter of good luck is how complacency starts. From the first of next month the alert covers every control on the map, manual or automatic, and no control leaves this desk without a named deputy.

gist.prompt: What is the best title for this note?
choices: A Formal Warning to the Owner of the Daily Check
Three Days, One Missing Step, and What Changes Now

items: The purpose of the note is to find the person who should be punished.
The note says it is blameless by design: it looks for the step that failed, not for the person who failed.
The breach was noticed by a trader who was looking for something else.
The note says a trader on the credit desk noticed it on Wednesday afternoon, by accident, while he was looking for something else.
The bank lost four million because of the breach.
The note says the market moved back on Thursday and they lost nothing, which is why it calls the event a near miss.
From next month the alert will cover manual controls as well as automatic ones.
The note says that from the first of next month the alert covers every control on the map, manual or automatic.

listenings.text: Sergio, it is Marina. You are presenting the post-mortem on Tuesday, and I want three things in your head before you walk in. First, keep it blameless, and I mean the words as well as the intention. The moment you say a name in the same sentence as the word failure, the room stops listening to the system and starts watching the person, and you will never get the honest version of anything again. Say the step failed. Never say Camila failed. Second, the room will want to know what would have happened, so give them one counterfactual, and only one you can defend. If the alert had covered manual controls, we would have seen it on Monday afternoon. That one is true and you can prove it. Do not say we would have caught it in an hour, because you do not know that, and somebody in that room will ask you how. Third, and this is the one people get wrong. A post-mortem that ends in hindsight is a story. A post-mortem that ends in a change is work. So finish with the two changes, with a date on each one, and with your name on both. And one last thing. Call it a near miss out loud. If you call it a small issue, the committee will file it and forget it, and next quarter we will be having this conversation with a number that hurts.

Sergio, Paulo here, from the credit desk. Two minutes on how people actually talk in a post-mortem, because the grammar carries more meaning than you think. There are three sentences in that room and each one does a different job. Should have is the one with a finger in it. We should have named the deputy. That is criticism, and it is fine when you point it at your own desk, and it is a bad idea when you point it at somebody else's. Would have is the result. If the alert had covered manual controls, we would have seen it on Monday. No blame in that one, just a consequence, and that is exactly why the auditors like it. Might have is the honest one. We might have caught it earlier. You are saying it was possible, not certain, and when you do not know, that is the sentence that keeps you credible. Now the two mistakes I hear every week from good speakers. The first one is putting would in the if half. Never if we would have known. It is if we had known. The would lives in the other half of the sentence, always. The second one is smaller and it is everywhere. When you say it fast it sounds like would of, and some people write it that way. It is not of, it is have. Would have, should have, could have. Say them out loud a few times tonight and it will stop sounding wrong on Tuesday.

extra_audio.text: First, put the timeline on the table: what happened, and at what time. Then name the step that failed, never the person who was on duty. Next, trace the problem back to the one lapse that started it. After that, say what would have happened if the missing step had run. Finally, name the change, put a date on it, and put your name next to it.
